scenes.title: Key ideas
items: Supply APY ≈ borrow APY × utilisation × (1 − reserve factor)

First, Utilisation equals borrowed divided by supplied. It drives the rates. Next, Interest-rate curve: most markets use a "kinked" curve. Rates rise gently. scenes.title: Worked example
scenes.vo: Near 100% utilisation, rates spike and lenders may not be able to withdraw, because the money is lent out. A sudden high supply A.P.Y. is often a warning, not a gift. 50%, 2.5%, 1.1%. 70%, 3.5%, 2.2%. 80%, 4.0%, 2.9%. 90%, 34.0%, 27.5%. 95%, 49.0%, 41.9%.

scenes.q: What sets the rates in a money market?
scenes.a: Mainly utilisation, through the protocol's interest-rate curve.
scenes.vo: Question one. What sets the rates in a money market? [[pause 4]] The answer: Mainly utilisation, through the protocol's interest-rate curve.
scenes.cap: Question 1. What sets the rates in a money market? The answer: Mainly utilisation, through the protocol's interest-rate curve.

scenes.a: To make borrowing expensive and supplying attractive when liquidity runs low, restoring withdrawal capacity.
scenes.vo: Question two. Why does the curve kink? [[pause 4]] The answer: To make borrowing expensive and supplying attractive when liquidity runs low, restoring withdrawal capacity.
scenes.cap: Question 2. Why does the curve kink? The answer: To make borrowing expensive and supplying attractive when liquidity runs low, restoring withdrawal capacity.

scenes.a: Withdrawals may be blocked until borrowers repay or new supply arrives.
scenes.vo: Question three. Utilisation is 99%. Risk for lenders? [[pause 4]] The answer: Withdrawals may be blocked until borrowers repay or new supply arrives.
